# Experiment 0024 — We have been measuring a doubles agent on singles teams

**Date:** 2026-08-30
**Result: the team pool every self-play measurement in this project rests on is generated by a *singles* format.** `gen9championsrandombattle` has no `gameType` in Showdown's format table, so it defaults to singles, and it is the only random generator Champions ships. The defining moves of VGC doubles — Tailwind, Trick Room, Rage Powder, Follow Me, Helping Hand — appear on **0.0%** of our generated teams and are used by humans in 6–31% of real battles. Protect: 89.4% of human battles, 22.0% of our teams.

Found while measuring the ceiling for backlog item 1, which was itself built on a broken comparison. Both are recorded here.

## The item that started it was wrong

Backlog item 1 claimed *"Protect is 14.5% of every move choice humans make in the corpus, and the agent picks it on roughly 0.2% of its own."* Both halves are true and the comparison between them is meaningless: it puts Protect's share of *all* move choices against Protect's share of *all* move choices in a pool where the agent usually does not have Protect at all.

Measured properly, against turns where Protect was actually on the sheet:

```
200 self-play battles
  turns Protect was on the sheet:    80      (0.40 per battle)
  used                                8      (10.0% of those turns)
  declined                           72      (90.0%)
```

The agent uses Protect on **10% of the turns it can**, not 0.2%. Protect is also *not* priced flat — `_score_protect` values it against the incoming threat, applies the engine's real stall counter (`1/3^streak`), and charges a tempo cost. The backlog said otherwise. Corrected.

## The pool is not the game

Humans use Protect **3.02 times per battle**, in **90.2% of battles**. Our agent is offered it 0.40 times per battle — **7.6× less often than humans use it.** That is far too large to be a decision-quality gap, so the teams were the obvious suspect.

Comparing how often our generated teams *carry* a move against how often humans *used* it. Human usage is a lower bound on human availability — a move brought but never clicked is invisible here — so every positive gap below is conservative:

```
move            humans used in    we carry in      gap
protect               89.4%          22.0%      +67.4%
fakeout               50.2%          12.5%      +37.7%
tailwind              31.4%           0.0%      +31.4%
trickroom             26.0%           0.0%      +26.0%
ragepowder            20.0%           0.0%      +20.0%
partingshot           17.2%           3.5%      +13.7%
helpinghand            8.8%           0.0%       +8.8%
followme               5.8%           0.0%       +5.8%

and the other way:
swordsdance            7.2%          57.5%      -50.3%
knockoff               8.4%          56.5%      -48.1%
earthquake            17.6%          62.0%      -44.4%
uturn                  0.6%          31.5%      -30.9%
stealthrock            0.2%          25.5%      -25.3%
dragondance            1.6%          30.5%      -28.9%
```

Redirection, speed control and support are absent; singles staples are everywhere. Stealth Rock is on a quarter of our teams and was used by humans in **one battle in five hundred** — it is an entry hazard in a format where nothing switches enough to care.

## Why, exactly

Showdown's format table settles it:

```ts
{
    name: "[Gen 9 Champions] Random Battle",
    mod: 'champions',
    team: 'random',          // <- no gameType, so singles
},
{
    name: "[Gen 9 Champions] VGC 2026 Reg M-B",
    mod: 'champions',
    gameType: 'doubles',     // <- no team, so players bring their own
},
```

The generator we call is a **singles** random-battle generator. The format we play is doubles. Champions ships no random doubles generator, so nothing was misconfigured — this is the only generator available, and its output was used without checking what distribution it produces. A singles set builder has no reason to ever pick Rage Powder, and it never did.

## What this does and does not touch

**Not affected — the engine-verified work.** Damage (94.8%), turn order (97.7%), the differential harness, the mechanics modules. These are checked against the engine's own arithmetic, which does not care which teams are on the field. This is the half of the project the backlog calls ground truth, and it stands.

**Not affected — the human-agreement benchmarks.** 0002, 0010 and 0013 score against reconstructed positions from real replays, so they already used real teams.

**Affected — every self-play win rate.** 0020's exchange rate of 0.23 points per point of damage accuracy, 0021's evaluator grading, 0022's search result, and 0023's null were all measured on this pool. 0023 is the sharpest example: it concluded setup is near break-even, measured on a pool where **57.5%** of teams carry Swords Dance against **7.2%** of human teams. The conclusion may well hold; it has not been tested where it matters.

**Affected — the heuristic's fitted constants**, wherever they were fitted on self-play rather than agreement.

## What a fix would need

Replays carry `|poke|` team-preview lines in all 500 battles — species, level, gender for all six — but `|showteam|` in only 3, so movesets, items and spreads are not directly available. They are recoverable in aggregate: `reconstruct.py` already assembles a player's own side from the whole log, so pooling observed sets per species across 500 battles gives usage-weighted movesets for the common ones. Partial by construction: a move that was never clicked was never seen.

Not attempted here. It is a change to the measuring instrument for the whole project, which is a decision rather than a task.

## Not established

- How much any past result would actually move on a realistic pool. That the distribution differs is measured; that specific conclusions flip is not.
- Whether corpus-harvested teams can be made complete enough to be worth switching to.
